name: Caramanta
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Extinct Chocoan variety; Glottolog lists only Aguirre Licht 2006 subclassification comments; no phonological description exists

new_statements.quote: Al hacer estas transcripciones es preciso anotar que en este vocabulario no hay acentos sino que todas las sílabas tienen igual fuerza; pero, como ocurre casi siempre, al pronunciar en esta forma una palabra cualquiera, queda la sensación de que la última sílaba recibió más fuerza; sólo en este sentido debe analizarse y entenderse todo acento ortográfico aquí marcado.
new_statements.translation: In making these transcriptions it must be noted that in this vocabulary there are no accents; rather, all syllables have equal force; but, as almost always happens, on pronouncing any word in this way one is left with the impression that the last syllable received more force; every orthographic accent marked here is to be analysed and understood only in that sense.
new_statements.citation: Daniel, H. 1954. Apuntes etnológicos: Los Caramantas. Boletín del Instituto de Antropología (Medellín) 1(2): 171-180.
new_statements.locator: p. 174, paragraph preceding 'Vocabulario tomado de los indios de la fracción de Cristianía'
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (5 PDF pages, each a two-page spread, text layer present; PDF p.3 = printed pp.174-175) and the page image. The passage is on printed p.174, left column, and matches the reported quote word for word (extracted text shows only line-break hyphenation: "vo-cabulario", ".fuer-za", "a-cento"): "Al hacer estas transcripciones es preciso anotar que en este vocabulario no hay acentos sino que todas las sílabas tienen igual fuerza; pero, como ocurre casi siempre, al pronunciar en esta forma una palabra cualquiera, queda la sensación de que la última sílaba recibió más fuerza; sólo en este sentido debe analizarse y entenderse todo acento ortográfico aquí marcad…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The collector (an ethnographer, not a linguist) reports no word accent: all syllables carry equal force, with a perceptual impression of final-syllable prominence; the few written accents in his list encode only that impression. If one reads the perceptual note as the stress fact, it amounts to final stress; the explicit claim is that there is no stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author warns the whole ~100-word list is unverified and invites specialists to check it.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms elicited in a brief visit; word level only. The 1876 Zeitschrift für Ethnologie report on 'embera bede' (which names the Caramantas among its speakers) only says accents were written where the author heard them (p.359), giving no rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand statement (Daniel 1954) describes the speech of the Cristianía settlement between Andes and Jardín, Antioquia — the community today known as Karmata Rua and identified as Emberá Chamí (Glottolog embe1262 Emberá-Chamí, ISO cmi; Glottolog otherwise files Chamí material under Northern Emberá nort2972). Daniel himself calls it 'idioma catío' (p.177), and his vocabulary (bania 'agua', boro 'cabeza', mukera 'hombre', numerals aba/ome/umpea/quimane/juasoma) is plainly Emberá; the same numerals are what Wikipedia cites from Arcila Vélez 1946 for 'Caramanta'. So the entity coded cara1271/crf as a distinct extinct Chocoan language is doubtful: the attested 'Caramanta' data are a 1940s-50s Emberá (Chamí/Catío) lect of the Caramanta region, and the stress note should be read as applying to that lect, not to an independent language.

sources.locator: p. 174, paragraph preceding 'Vocabulario tomado de los indios de la fracción de Cristianía'
sources.note: p.174, prefacing a ~100-word vocabulary taken at Cristianía (between Andes and Jardín, Antioquia): in this vocabulary there are no accents, all syllables have equal force, but on pronouncing any word one is left with the impression that the last syllable received more force; every orthographic accent marked is to be read only in that sense. p.177 'Observaciones' calls the language 'idioma catío'; the numerals aba/ome/umpea/quimane/juasoma are Emberá.

sources.citation: Harms, Phillip L. (comp.). 1989 [table pages dated July 1990]. Comparative Word List of Chocoan Languages. Prepublication draft. SIL Language and Culture Archives, 33 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Scan without text layer; scanned of pp.2-4 (the page imageharms-0[234]) shows the varieties covered are Chamí, Catío, Darién, Saija, Tadó, Basurudó, Waunan — Caramanta is not included. Nothing on stress on the pages scanned.

States the language is documented solely through the 1940s wordlist (Arcila Vélez 1946) and Daniel 1954; sometimes treated as a dialect of Anserma (Ethnologue 25). Its Caramanta numerals aba, ome, umpea, quimane, juasoma are identical to Daniel 1954 p.177. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Anon. [signed 'B.' in editorial footnote]. 1876. Bericht über die Sprache, welche die Chamies-, Angáguedas-, Murindoes-, Cañasgordas-, Rioverdes-, Necodaes-, Caramantas-, Tadocitos-, Patoes- und Curasambas-Indianer sprechen. Zeitschrift für Ethnologie 8: 359-378.

sources.note: Language called 'embera bede', common to all the listed groups (incl. Caramantas) with dialectal deviations; Glottolog files this item under Northern Emberá nort2972. p.359 'Allgemeine Bemerkungen / Zeichen': the only diacritics mark teeth-clenched and nasal syllables; '[Zur] Accentuation ist der Accent dahin gesetzt, wo ich das Wort habe betonen hören' — accent written wherever the author heard the word stressed; no placement rule given.
